Q1259987.title: Exsurge Domine
paras: Pope Leo X had authorised a large sale of indulgences, partly to pay for the rebuilding of St Peter's in Rome, and Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against its abuses in 1517 had set off a revolt across Germany. Neither the papal legate Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg in 1518 nor a papal bull on indulgences had made Luther retract, and at the Leipzig Debate of 1519 Johann Eck had drawn him into open rejection of papal authority. In January 1520 a commission met in Rome to examine Luther's teachings. Eck joined it halfway through, bringing the condemnations of Luther issued by the universities of Cologne and Leuven, and he pressed it towards a quick and sweeping verdict.

The commission, of some forty cardinals, theologians and canon lawyers, was divided: some feared that condemning so popular a figure was politically dangerous, the theologians wanted immediate condemnation, and the canon lawyers wanted Luther to be heard first. The compromise gave him no hearing but sixty days to recant. Instead of answering each point, the text simply listed forty-one propositions from Luther's writings, more than half from the Ninety-five Theses and their defence and much of the rest from the Leipzig Debate, and condemned them all together as heretical, scandalous, false, offensive to pious ears or misleading to simple minds. Leo X added a preface, which opens with the words Exsurge Domine ('Arise, O Lord') and calls on God to rise against a wild boar ravaging his vineyard, and issued the bull on 15 June 1520.

According to its text as Wikipedia quotes it, the bull ordered Luther's books to be burned and threatened him and his supporters, among them Andreas Karlstadt, with excommunication unless they recanted within sixty days of its publication in Saxony and the neighbouring lands. Eck took it to Germany as papal nuncio and published it with two papal legates, but bishops, universities and humanists alike denounced it; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says Eck was lucky to escape from Saxony unharmed. Luther refused to recant, attacked the papacy in new pamphlets and on 10 December 1520 publicly burned a copy of the bull at the Elster Gate in Wittenberg. On 3 January 1521 Leo X excommunicated him with the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem.

Q1425362.title: Battle of Cajamarca
paras: Francisco Pizarro, licensed by Charles V in 1529 to conquer the coast he had explored, sailed from Panama in January 1531 with three ships, 180 men and 27 horses, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He reached the Inca Empire just as Atahualpa had won a civil war against his half-brother Huáscar, whom his commanders had just captured. Atahualpa was camped outside the highland town of Cajamarca with an army that Wikipedia puts at nearly 80,000 veterans, and he let the small Spanish force come inland, apparently confident that it could do him no harm. The Spaniards entered the half-empty town on 15 November 1532. Unable either to attack such an army or to retreat safely, Pizarro planned to seize the emperor himself, as Cortés had seized Moctezuma.

On the afternoon of 16 November Atahualpa came into the town's great square, carried on a litter lined with parrot feathers and plated with gold and silver, with thousands of richly dressed attendants who were unarmed or carried only ceremonial weapons; his main army stayed outside the town. The Spaniards were hidden in the buildings round the square, with horsemen in the alleys and guns in a central stone building. The friar Vicente de Valverde came out with an interpreter and called on Atahualpa to accept the Christian faith. Pizarro's secretary Francisco de Xerez, an eyewitness, says the Inca threw down the book he was handed and complained of how the Spaniards had treated his people on their march; Spanish sources differ on exactly what set off the fighting.

At the signal the guns fired and the horsemen and infantry charged out. The attendants offered almost no resistance; many died shielding the litter, and the crowd fleeing the square broke down part of its wall. Pizarro reached the litter and seized Atahualpa, receiving a cut on the hand while protecting him from his own men. The Inca army outside the town scattered. Thousands of Atahualpa's nobles, counsellors and attendants were killed; most sources say no Spaniard died.

The capture began the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire. To buy his freedom Atahualpa promised, Xerez records, to fill a room 22 feet long and 17 wide with gold up to a line half way up the wall, and twice with silver. The ransom was gathered and shared out among the conquerors, but Atahualpa was not freed: sentenced to death on a charge of treason, which the 19th-century translator Clements Markham calls a false pretext, he was baptised and then strangled at Cajamarca in 1533.

Q2091449.title: Battle of Mactan
paras: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain, had left Spain in 1519 to find a western route to the Spice Islands. After crossing the Pacific his fleet sighted Samar on 16 March 1521 and on 7 April reached Cebu. There Rajah Humabon accepted baptism, taking the name Carlos after the Spanish king, and became Magellan's ally; at Magellan's urging the neighbouring chiefs were told to supply the ships and to accept Christianity. On the small island of Mactan, beside the harbour where the fleet lay, the chief Lapulapu (Cilapulapu in the account of the voyage's chronicler, Antonio Pigafetta) refused to submit to Humabon or to the king of Spain. Mactan's other chief, Zula, sent Magellan a son with two goats and asked for a boatload of men to help him against Lapulapu.

Against the pleas of his officers, Magellan decided to lead the attack himself. Pigafetta writes that sixty men in corselets and helmets set out at midnight in three boats, with Humabon and twenty or thirty local boats, and reached Mactan three hours before dawn on Saturday, 27 April. Magellan offered friendship if the islanders would obey the king of Spain, recognise Humabon as their sovereign and pay tribute; they answered that they had lances of bamboo and stakes hardened in fire. Rocks kept the boats far from the shore, so at daybreak 49 men waded in up to their thighs while 11 guarded the boats. Magellan had told Humabon to stay in his boat and watch.

On the beach, Pigafetta says, more than 1,500 warriors in three divisions attacked the landing party from the front and both flanks. The musketeers and crossbowmen fired uselessly from too far off for about half an hour, and when Magellan had houses set on fire the defenders grew only more furious. Shot in the right leg with a poisoned arrow, he ordered a slow withdrawal, but most of his men fled, leaving six or eight with him; aiming at their bare legs, the islanders drove them back into knee-deep water, where they fought for more than an hour. Wounded in the arm by a bamboo spear so that he could not draw his sword, and then cut in the left leg by a large sword (probably a kampilan, according to Wikipedia), Magellan fell and was killed. Pigafetta counts eight Europeans killed with him, four Christian islanders killed by the boats' own guns, and fifteen of the enemy dead.

Lapulapu's people refused to give up Magellan's body for any amount of goods. Days later Humabon turned on his allies: Wikipedia says survivors were poisoned at a feast he gave, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that he seized and murdered several leaders, among them Juan Serrano, one of the two commanders chosen to replace Magellan. The survivors burned one of their three ships and left the Philippines; the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reached Spain in 1522, completing the first voyage around the world. In the Philippines the battle is remembered as the first victory of a native Filipino over Spanish forces, and Lapulapu as the country's first national hero; in 2017, 27 April was declared Lapulapu Day.

Q2558706.title: Francis Drake's circumnavigation
Q2558706.place: Plymouth, England, and around the world
paras: Francis Drake was an English seaman who had sailed with his kinsman John Hawkins against the Spanish at San Juan de Ulúa in the Caribbean and had raided Spanish Panama in 1572–1573, when he first saw the Pacific. Protestant England did not accept the Spanish and Portuguese division of the world under the Treaty of Tordesillas, and relations between Queen Elizabeth I and Philip II of Spain were deteriorating. With the queen's backing Drake proposed a voyage through the Strait of Magellan into the Pacific, where no Englishman had yet sailed. Officially a voyage of discovery, it was in effect a covert raiding expedition against Spain's Pacific coast.

Five small ships with about 164 men (166 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica) left Plymouth in November 1577 but were driven back by a storm, and sailed again on 13 December. At Port St Julian in Patagonia Drake had Thomas Doughty, one of his company, tried and beheaded for plotting against him. He renamed his flagship, the Pelican, the Golden Hind and entered the Strait of Magellan in August 1578, but storms in the Pacific scattered the fleet: the Marigold was lost, presumably with all hands, and the Elizabeth under John Wynter returned to England, leaving the Golden Hind alone.

Drake sailed up the coast of Chile and Peru, plundering Spanish towns and ships, and on 1 March 1579 captured the treasure ship Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, laden with silver. To avoid the Spanish, who were now hunting him, he sailed north in search of a passage back to the Atlantic, then landed in what is now northern California to repair his ship; he named the land New Albion and claimed it for Elizabeth. In late July 1579 he set out across the Pacific, reached the Moluccas, where the sultan of Ternate received him well and he traded for about ten tonnes of spices, mostly cloves; after the ship struck a rock off Celebes and was got off again, he went on to Java, rounded the Cape of Good Hope in June 1580 and reached Plymouth on 26 September 1580 with 59 men and a rich cargo of spices and Spanish treasure.

Drake was the first Englishman to sail round the world and the first captain since Magellan's expedition to complete a circumnavigation in his own ship. After some hesitation, for fear of trouble with Spain, the queen knighted him aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford on 4 April 1581, to the anger of Philip II, who regarded him as a pirate. The voyage was one of the causes of the Anglo-Spanish War of 1585–1604, and Spain answered Drake's entry into the Pacific by trying to colonise the Strait of Magellan to close it.

Q371558.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
paras: John Calvin, a young French scholar trained in law and classics, became a Protestant around 1533, at a time when the reform movement was persecuted in France, and had to go into hiding. He began the studies that led to his great book while staying at Angoulême in 1534, and in 1535 took refuge in Basel, then a centre of Protestant learning. King Francis I, who was persecuting Protestants at home but wanted to stay on good terms with the Lutheran princes of Germany against Charles V, had his envoys explain that he was punishing only Anabaptists and other enemies of all civil government. Calvin was indignant at this slur on the French reformers and rushed his work into print.

The Institutes of the Christian Religion (Institutio Christianae Religionis) was published in Latin at Basel in March 1536, so that it could reach educated readers in every country. It opened with a letter to Francis I asking him to give the Protestants a hearing instead of persecuting them, and presenting the book as their confession of faith. The first edition was a short manual in six chapters, following the traditional order of religious teaching: the Law (the Ten Commandments), faith (the Apostles' Creed), prayer and the sacraments, followed by chapters on the 'false sacraments' and on Christian liberty, church power and civil government. It drew on Luther for faith and the sacraments and on Martin Bucer of Strasbourg for predestination. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that Calvin was only twenty-six when it appeared.

The book was an immediate success, and Calvin, who soon afterwards began his ministry in Geneva, kept enlarging it. A much larger Latin edition appeared in 1539 and further ones in 1543 and 1550, and he also translated it into French: Wikipedia dates the first French edition to 1541, while the Britannica says the earliest known one is of 1540. The final Latin edition of 1559, which scholars treat as the authoritative text, is 80% larger than the one before it, yet Calvin's essential ideas did not change. The Institutes became the core statement of the doctrine of the Reformed churches, usually called Calvinism, and one of the most influential works of Protestant theology.

Q593267.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
paras: Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Mexica (Aztecs) in Lake Texcoco, fell after a two-year struggle with the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés. Cortés had landed on the Gulf coast in April 1519 with 508 soldiers, 100 sailors and 14 small cannon, and won allies among peoples who resented Aztec rule, above all the Tlaxcalans. Received in Tenochtitlan, he made the emperor Moctezuma his prisoner. When he left the city to defeat a Spanish force sent from Cuba to arrest him, his lieutenant Pedro de Alvarado provoked a rising. Moctezuma died, and the Spaniards fought their way out of the city at night, an escape remembered as La Noche Triste; by the time they reached Tlaxcala, Wikipedia says, they had lost more than 860 Spanish soldiers and over a thousand Tlaxcalans. On the way they beat a large Aztec army at Otumba, on 7 July 1520 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

While Cortés rebuilt his forces, a smallpox epidemic, to which the Spaniards were largely immune, swept the Valley of Mexico and killed many Aztec leaders; Cuauhtémoc became emperor in February 1521. Cortés had thirteen brigantines built in pieces at Tlaxcala and launched on the lake from Texcoco, gathered reinforcements and tens of thousands of native warriors, and won over the lakeside towns. On 22 May 1521 three columns under Alvarado, Cristóbal de Olid and Gonzalo de Sandoval took up positions at the heads of the causeways, cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec that brought much of the city's water, and the brigantines scattered the Aztec canoe fleet.

The siege lasted about three months. The Aztecs fought street by street; in one counter-attack Cortés was wounded and almost captured, and sixty-five Spaniards were taken alive and sacrificed in sight of their comrades. Cortés answered by razing each district he took and using the rubble to fill the canals, so that his cavalry and infantry could advance in formation, while the blockade starved the city: its people ate wood and leather and drank brackish water, and disease spread. The attackers finally reached the market square of Tlatelolco. Cuauhtémoc tried to escape by canoe but was captured by Sandoval's brigantines, and the Aztecs surrendered on 13 August 1521, the date also given by the Britannica.

The fall of the city destroyed the Aztec state and was a critical stage in Spain's colonisation of the Americas. Wikipedia gives estimates of 100,000 to 240,000 killed in the campaign as a whole, warriors and civilians together; almost all the Aztec nobility died, and Spain's native allies, mainly the Tlaxcalans, went on killing and looting after the surrender.

Q645920.title: Protestation at Speyer
paras: Martin Luther had been placed under the ban of the Holy Roman Empire by the Edict of Worms in 1521, but the edict was not enforced everywhere. In 1526 the first Diet of Speyer resolved that, until a church council met, each state should conduct its religious affairs as it hoped to answer for them to God and the emperor, and the Lutheran princes took this as licence to organise their own territorial churches. In 1529 Emperor Charles V, at war with France, called a second diet at Speyer and was represented by his brother Ferdinand. Ferdinand announced that the emperor annulled the 1526 decision; according to Wikipedia's account of his declarations, further innovations were forbidden until a council, the Mass was to be refused to no one, and neither those who rejected the real presence of Christ in the sacrament nor the Anabaptists were to be tolerated.

The Catholic majority of the diet accepted the revocation on 19 April 1529 and told the evangelical estates to yield to it. The evangelical princes left the hall, and when they returned Ferdinand refused to hear them, so their objection was read out: they would keep to the decision of 1526 and would not be bound by the majority in matters of faith. On 20 April they presented a formal Letter of Protestation, which Ferdinand refused to accept; it was printed and published instead. Its signers were Elector John of Saxony, Margrave George of Brandenburg-Ansbach, Duke Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg, Landgrave Philip of Hesse and Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt, joined by representatives of 14 imperial free cities, among them Strasbourg and Ulm.

When the diet's decree was read again at its last sitting on 24 April without mention of the protest, the princes' councillors and the cities' agents drew up a formal appeal on 25 April and sent it to the emperor by an embassy. From this protest the reformers took the name Protestants, and the event is often counted as the birth of Protestantism. As the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica observes, a minority could hold to such a protest only if it was ready to defend itself by force, and three days after the protest was read many of the protesting cities and states made a secret treaty, while Philip of Hesse began to work for a general union of the evangelical states.

Q661327.title: Battle of Mühlberg
Q661327.place: Mühlberg on the Elbe, Saxony, Germany
paras: The battle was the decisive clash of the Schmalkaldic War between Emperor Charles V and the Schmalkaldic League, the defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities led by Elector John Frederick of Saxony and Landgrave Philip of Hesse. For years Charles had tolerated the league while he fought France and the Ottomans, but the Treaty of Crépy with France in 1544 freed his hands. The war began in 1546 when Maurice of Saxony, a Protestant cousin and rival of John Frederick who had refused to join the league, invaded the elector's lands with the help of Charles's brother Ferdinand. John Frederick drove him back, but the emperor joined the war, occupied Ulm and Württemberg, forced the Elector Palatine to submit, and in spring 1547 marched into Saxony.

John Frederick had sent much of his army to Bohemia, hoping for a Protestant rising there, and was withdrawing north towards his fortress of Wittenberg. He camped at Mühlberg, leaving only a few guards on the Elbe, which he thought too wide for the imperial army to cross quickly. Charles, so ill with gout that he was carried in a litter, reached the river on the evening of 23 April and, against his generals' advice, decided to attack. At dawn on 24 April, under cover of fog, Spanish and Italian veterans swam the river and overcame the Saxon guards; a local farmer showed the Duke of Alba's men a ford, and the cavalry crossed by a pontoon bridge that the Saxons had failed to destroy.

Taken by surprise, the elector drew up his army along the edge of a forest. The imperial cavalry under Alba and Maurice broke the Saxon wings, and the infantry tercios in the centre drove the Protestants back into the forest. John Frederick fought bravely but was wounded in the face and captured. Wikipedia puts the Saxon losses at 2,000 to 3,000 men, with nearly all their artillery and banners taken, against about fifty imperial dead.

The victory decided the war in the emperor's favour, and the league was dissolved. Charles spared John Frederick's life in exchange for the surrender of Wittenberg, but kept him prisoner and transferred his electoral title to Maurice; Philip of Hesse submitted soon afterwards. The success did not last: within a few years a new conflict broke out, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 allowed each ruler to choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism.

Q688998.title: Leipzig Debate
paras: Two years after Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, the quarrel had become a contest between named champions. Johann Eck, professor of theology at Ingolstadt and a famous debater, had in 1518 circulated a privately written attack, the Obelisci, branding Luther a Hussite, a follower of Jan Hus, whose teachings the Council of Constance had condemned. Andreas Karlstadt, dean of the theology faculty at Wittenberg, took up Luther's defence, answered Eck in a long series of theses and challenged him to a public debate. Eck accepted, and the debate was held in June and July 1519 in the Pleissenburg castle at Leipzig, in the presence of Duke George of Saxony, himself an opponent of Luther.

According to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eck first debated Karlstadt on 27 and 28 June and 1 and 3 July on grace, free will and good works. From 4 to 14 July he faced Luther, and the subject widened to purgatory, indulgences, penance and, above all, the authority of the pope. Eck's aim was to push Luther into a statement that would let his opponents identify him with Hus, and he succeeded: Luther conceded that some of Hus's opinions were true and declared himself against the papacy.

The judges gave no verdict, but the general impression, says the Britannica, was that Eck had won, and Luther went back to Wittenberg depressed. Yet the debate made Luther see that his protest struck at the centre of the church's system, not at an abuse on its edge. His published account rallied support in Germany, and in 1520 he wrote his three great reforming treatises. Eck, meanwhile, went to Rome, and the papal bull Exsurge Domine of June 1520, which he helped to prepare, followed the line of his charges at Leipzig and threatened Luther with excommunication.

Q691882.title: Münster rebellion
paras: The Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and baptised adult believers again, and some of them expected the end of the world to be near. After the Peasants' War of 1524–1525 their most radical wing made a new attempt to set up a kingdom of the saints at Münster in Westphalia, a city of the prince-bishopric of Münster in the Holy Roman Empire. There the Lutheran preacher Bernhard Rothmann, backed by the wealthy wool merchant Bernhard Knipperdolling, moved from attacking Catholicism to preaching the equality of all believers, including in property. Followers of Jan Matthys, a baker from Haarlem, among them the tailor Jan Bockelson (John of Leiden), declared Münster the New Jerusalem; from 5 January 1534 adult baptism spread quickly, and in February the Anabaptists won control of the city council and made Knipperdolling mayor.

Many Lutherans left and Anabaptists arrived from outside. Rebaptism was made compulsory, churches and monasteries were stripped of images, and property was declared common. The expelled bishop, Franz von Waldeck, laid siege to the city. At Easter 1534 Matthys, who had prophesied God's judgement for that day and saw himself as a second Gideon, went out against the besiegers with a handful of men and was killed with all of them: twelve followers according to Wikipedia, thirty according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

John of Leiden took his place, claimed visions from heaven, proclaimed himself the successor of King David with royal honours and absolute power, and made polygamy legal. Wikipedia says he took sixteen wives, the Britannica four; both report that he beheaded one of them in the market place, though Wikipedia notes that this may have been attributed to him falsely. As the siege dragged on, most of the people starved. After a long resistance the besiegers took the city on 24 June 1535. In January 1536 John of Leiden, Knipperdolling and Bernhard Krechting were tortured and executed in the market place, and their bodies were hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert's Church, where the cages still hang.

Münster was the turning point of the Anabaptist movement: after it, Catholic and Lutheran rulers alike suppressed the Anabaptists harshly, and they never again had political weight. The peaceful Anabaptists who followed Menno Simons, the Mennonites, rejected the doctrines of the Münster radicals.

cp04-16.title: First circumnavigation completed (Magellan–Elcano expedition)
paras: The expedition was a Spanish venture, paid for mostly by King Charles I, to reach the Moluccas, the Spice Islands, by sailing west, since the eastern route around Africa belonged to Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas. Its commander, the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan, left Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 20 September 1519 with five ships and about 270 men. The fleet passed through the strait at the tip of South America that now bears his name late in 1520 and crossed the Pacific in 98 days, the crews eating ox-hides, sawdust and rats as scurvy spread.

Magellan was killed in a fight on Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521, and soon afterwards many of his officers were murdered on Cebu. The survivors burned one ship and reached Tidore in the Moluccas in November 1521, where they loaded cloves. The flagship Trinidad was found to be leaking and stayed behind (it was later captured by the Portuguese), so on 21 December 1521 the Victoria, commanded by the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, set out for Spain alone by the Portuguese route across the Indian Ocean.

The homeward voyage was a race against hunger. With only rice to eat, the Victoria rounded the Cape of Good Hope on 6 May 1522 after weeks of storms. By 9 July, when Elcano put into the Portuguese Cape Verde Islands for food, twenty men had died according to Wikipedia (twenty-one, counting Europeans and Moluccans, according to the voyage's chronicler Antonio Pigafetta). There the crew discovered that their carefully kept log was a day behind the islanders' calendar, the day gained by sailing round the world westward. When the Portuguese learned where the ship had been, they seized thirteen men ashore and the Victoria fled.

On Saturday 6 September 1522 the Victoria entered the bay of Sanlúcar with 18 men, most of them sick, almost three years after setting out; two days later they anchored at Seville and went barefoot with candles to give thanks at its shrines. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 31 men as returning with Elcano. The men held in Cape Verde were later released, and a few survivors of the Trinidad came home years later. The voyage was the first circumnavigation of the Earth and the first European crossing of the Pacific, and it showed both the vastness of that ocean and that the world could be sailed round by a western sea route.

cp04-18.title: Jacques Cartier explores the Gulf of St. Lawrence
cp04-18.place: Gulf of St. Lawrence (Newfoundland, Gaspé), Canada
paras: Jacques Cartier was a navigator from Saint-Malo in Brittany. Introduced to King Francis I by the bishop of Saint-Malo, Jean Le Veneur, he was commissioned to look for a western passage to the riches of Asia and for lands said to hold gold. France had already sent Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the North American coast in 1524. Cartier sailed from Saint-Malo on 20 April 1534 with two ships and, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, sixty-one men.

He reached Newfoundland on 10 May after twenty days at sea and entered the Strait of Belle Isle. Turning south, he followed the west coast of Newfoundland into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, passed the Bird Rocks, where his crew killed about 1,000 birds, most of them great auks, and named Brion Island after Admiral Chabot. He took the Magdalen Islands and Prince Edward Island for the mainland, and was disappointed to find that Chaleur Bay was not a strait. On its north shore he met and traded briefly with local people, probably Mi'kmaq.

In Gaspé Bay he met a party of St. Lawrence Iroquoians from the Quebec region. There, on 24 July, he set up a tall cross inscribed 'Long live the King of France', claiming the land for Francis I, and he took two sons of their chief Donnacona back with him; Wikipedia describes this as a kidnapping to which the chief at last consented on condition that they return with goods to trade. He then coasted round Anticosti Island, mistaking the channel to the north of it for a bay, and on finding it a council decided to leave its exploration to the next year. He left the Gulf through the Strait of Belle Isle on 15 August and reached Saint-Malo on 5 September 1534, convinced that he had reached an Asian land.

The voyage opened the way for French claims in North America. In 1535 Cartier returned with three ships, 110 men and his two captives, who guided him up the St. Lawrence to Donnacona's town of Stadacona and on to Hochelaga, the site of Montreal, which he reached on 2 October 1535. The captives' word for a village, kanata, gave Canada its name.

cp05-09.title: Schmalkaldic League formed
paras: Soon after the start of the Reformation, the Lutheran princes and cities of the Holy Roman Empire looked for protection against their Catholic emperor, Charles V. At the town of Schmalkalden they formally concluded a defensive alliance on 27 February 1531, pledging to defend one another if the emperor attacked their lands. Its leaders were Landgrave Philip of Hesse and the house of Saxony: the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913 lists Elector John of Saxony and his son John Frederick among the parties, while Wikipedia names John Frederick as co-founder with Philip. Other founding members included Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt, dukes of Brunswick, the counts of Mansfeld and cities such as Strasbourg, Ulm, Constance, Magdeburg and Bremen. At Saxony's insistence, members had to accept the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession.

According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, the members bound themselves for six years to treat an attack on any one of them, on account of religion or on any other pretext, as an attack on all. Saxony and Hesse were made its military commanders, and the league's forces were fixed at 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. It sought foreign allies, among them France, and later Denmark. In December 1535 it was renewed for ten years and opened to all who accepted the Augsburg Confession; Württemberg, Pomerania, Anhalt and cities such as Augsburg and Frankfurt joined.

Charles V was tied down for years by wars with France and the Ottoman Empire, and the threat from the Ottomans led his brother Ferdinand to grant the Protestants a religious peace at Nuremberg in July 1532. Under the league's protection its members spread Lutheranism across northern Germany, confiscating church lands and expelling bishops; in 1542 they drove the Catholic Duke Henry out of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Once Charles had made peace with France he turned on the league. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 his forces routed the league's army at Mühlberg on 24 April 1547 and captured John Frederick, and the league was dissolved. The defeat proved temporary: a Protestant victory in 1552 led to the Peace of Passau and three years later to the Peace of Augsburg, which gave Lutheranism official status in the Empire.

cp05-13.title: Society of Jesus approved
paras: The Society of Jesus grew from a group of students at the University of Paris around Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque from Spain and a former soldier. On 15 August 1534 Ignatius and six companions, among them Francis Xavier, Peter Faber, Diego Laínez and Simão Rodrigues, met in a crypt at Montmartre and vowed themselves to poverty and chastity (Wikipedia adds obedience; the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913 names only poverty and chastity, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates their vow to obey an elected superior to 1539). They hoped to go to the Holy Land, but war made the journey impossible. In 1537 they went to Italy, where Pope Paul III allowed them to be ordained priests, and they gave themselves to preaching and charitable work. When the hope of Jerusalem was finally given up, they agreed on a common rule and the name Company of Jesus.

Ignatius, Faber and Laínez then offered their services to the pope in Rome. Paul III received them well, but their plan met strong opposition: a commission of cardinals had just reported that the existing religious orders had decayed so badly that they should all be abolished, and Cardinal Guidiccioni, who examined the draft, wanted no new orders. Ignatius's idea of priests who would live in the world, with no distinctive habit or enclosure, also broke with tradition. In 1539 the companions bound themselves to obey a superior elected from among them and added a special vow of obedience to the pope for missions. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits King John III of Portugal, who wanted Jesuits for Portugal and its Indian possessions, with helping to change Guidiccioni's mind.

On 27 September 1540 Paul III confirmed the new society with the bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae, which, as the Britannica quotes it, set out Ignatius's formula: the society existed to spread the faith by preaching, the Spiritual Exercises, works of charity and the teaching of children and the uneducated, and all its members served under obedience to the pope. The bull limited the society to sixty members, a restriction removed, according to Wikipedia, by Julius III in 1550, but according to the Britannica by Paul III himself in 1543. Ignatius was chosen as the first superior general.

The Jesuits became an important force in the Counter-Reformation and in Catholic missions. Francis Xavier, sent to Portugal in March 1540, left Europe for the Indian mission the next year, and the society went on to found colleges and missions across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

cp18-098.title: Khanate of Khiva founded
cp18-098.place: Khwarazm (Vazir, Urgench and Khiva), Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
paras: At the start of the 16th century Khwarazm (Khorezm), the irrigated oasis of the lower Amu Darya south of the Aral Sea, changed hands several times. It had been nominally subject to the Timurid sultan Husayn Bayqara of Khorasan until 1505, when it was taken by Muhammad Shaybani, the leader of the Uzbeks, who had overthrown Timurid rule in Transoxiana. In 1510 Shaybani was defeated and killed near Merv by Shah Ismail I, the founder of Shia Safavid Persia, and Khwarazm passed to the shah. According to the 19th-century historian Henry Howorth, who followed the chronicle of the later Khivan khan Abu'l-Ghazi, Ismail put three Persian governors over its towns: one at Urgench, the capital, one over Khiva and Hazarasp, and one at Vazir.

The Sunni townspeople and tribes resented the Shia governors. Howorth relates that the people of Vazir, urged on by a holy man named Husamuddin Katal, secretly invited Ilbars, the son of the Uzbek chief Bereke Sultan, to become their khan. The conspirators seized the town gates and massacred the Persians inside; only one escaped. Ilbars was proclaimed khan at a feast of Uzbeks and Sarts and made Vazir his residence. Three months later he defeated the Persian governor of Urgench, Sultan Kuli, outside that town and took it, and he called in kinsmen and their tribes from the Kipchak steppe, whose raids made the Persian garrisons give up Khiva and Hazarasp. Wikipedia dates the expulsion of the shah's garrison and Ilbars's accession to 1511, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the start of Uzbek rule in Khiva to 1512. Abu'l-Ghazi gives the year 911 of the Hijra, which Howorth rejects because the rising came after Shaybani's death; he suggests it may have been 921.

Ilbars and his kin were themselves Shaybanids, but of a rival line. Their dynasty, the Arabshahids or Yadigarids, was named after Arabshah and his descendant Yadigar, who had been proclaimed khan north of the Aral Sea in about 1458 (Wikipedia); Howorth adds that Ilbars's father Bereke Sultan had been hunted down and killed by Muhammad Shaybani himself. The new state was therefore a second Uzbek khanate and a rival of the Shaybanid khanate of Bukhara up the river.

From Khwarazm the Uzbeks raided Khorasan and the Turkmens, especially after Shah Ismail's death. The capital stayed at Urgench until about 1600, when a branch of the Amu Darya dried up and Arab Muhammad Khan (1602–1623) moved it to Khiva, which gave the state its later name. The khanate fought repeated wars with Bukhara, was occupied by Nader Shah of Persia in 1740–1746, came under the Qongrat dynasty and became a Russian protectorate in 1873. It lasted until 1920, when it was replaced by the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic.

Q1785022.title: Bohemian Revolt
Q1785022.place: Prague and the lands of the Bohemian Crown, Czech Republic
paras: The Kingdom of Bohemia had been ruled by Habsburg kings since 1526, but its estates (the nobles and towns represented in the diet) were overwhelmingly Protestant: mostly Utraquist Hussites, with many Lutherans among the German population. In 1609 Emperor Rudolf II had granted them freedom of worship in his Letter of Majesty. His childless brother and successor Matthias had his cousin Ferdinand, Duke of Styria, a fervent Catholic who had suppressed Protestantism in Styria, accepted by the estates in 1617 as the next king of Bohemia. Protestant leaders feared that Ferdinand would take away the Letter's protections, and a dispute broke out over Protestant churches built on the lands of Catholic church lords, which the Catholic authorities ordered closed and the Protestants held were covered by the Letter.

In May 1618 the Protestant members of the diet gathered in Prague. On 23 May a group of them, led by Count Jindřich Matyáš Thurn, went up to the royal chancellery in Prague Castle, accused two of the king's Catholic regents, Jaroslav Bořita of Martinice and Vilém Slavata of Chlum, of having turned the emperor against them, and threw both men and their secretary Philip Fabricius out of the windows. All three survived the fall. This Defenestration of Prague began the revolt. The estates set up a provisional government of thirty 'directors' (ten from each estate, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica) and raised an army under Thurn; fighting with imperial troops began that summer, and a mercenary force under Ernst von Mansfeld, sent with the backing of Frederick V, the Calvinist Elector Palatine, took Pilsen in November 1618.

Matthias died in March 1619. Moravia, Silesia and the Lusatias joined the Bohemians, and in June Thurn advanced to the walls of Vienna, though he soon withdrew. At the end of July the lands of the Bohemian Crown formed a confederation, and Ferdinand was declared deposed as king of Bohemia (on 31 July according to the Britannica's Bohemia article; in August according to Wikipedia and the Britannica's article on Frederick V). On 26 August 1619 the estates elected Frederick V as their king; two days later Ferdinand was elected Holy Roman Emperor at Frankfurt.

The rebels found few friends. The Protestant Union of German princes stayed out, and the Lutheran Elector of Saxony sided with Ferdinand in return for Lusatia. Ferdinand also won Maximilian of Bavaria, leader of the Catholic League, and help from Spain, whose troops under Ambrogio Spinola invaded Frederick's own lands on the Rhine. In the autumn of 1620 an imperial and League army under Maximilian, Count Tilly and Count Bucquoy entered Bohemia, and on 8 November 1620 it routed the Bohemian army in a few hours at the White Mountain outside Prague. Frederick, mocked as the 'Winter King', fled the city.

Bohemia submitted almost without resistance. Twenty-seven rebel leaders were executed in Prague's Old Town Square on 21 June 1621, the lands of those who had joined the revolt were confiscated, much of the old Protestant nobility went into exile, and Protestants were forced to convert or leave. A decree of Ferdinand (dated 1627 by the Britannica) made the Bohemian crown hereditary in the Habsburg house and gave German equal standing with Czech in government offices and courts. Frederick was put under the imperial ban and his electoral title passed to Maximilian. The fighting did not end there: the revolt became the first phase of the Thirty Years' War.

cp06-02.title: Bohemian estates elect Frederick V king
paras: After the Defenestration of Prague in May 1618 the rebel Bohemian estates still had to settle who would be their king. Emperor Matthias died in March 1619, and the estates refused to accept his designated heir, the Catholic Ferdinand of Styria, whom they had recognised in 1617. At the end of July Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and the Lusatias joined in a confederation, and Ferdinand was declared deposed. The Elector of Saxony, the estates' preferred Protestant candidate, let it be known that he would not take the crown. That left Frederick V, the 23-year-old Calvinist Elector Palatine: head of the Protestant Union of German princes founded by his father, son-in-law of James I of England through his marriage to Elizabeth Stuart in 1613, and already in touch with the rebels, whom he had helped by sending a mercenary force under Ernst von Mansfeld.

On 26 August 1619 the estates of the confederation elected Frederick king of Bohemia. Two days later, at Frankfurt, the electors chose Ferdinand as Holy Roman Emperor; according to Wikipedia, Frederick's was the only vote against him. Frederick hesitated. The Protestant Union, meeting at Rothenburg on 12 September, urged him not to intervene, his father-in-law James was against it, and other possible allies told him not to expect help; only Gabriel Bethlen, the Prince of Transylvania, who had risen against the Habsburgs in Hungary, encouraged him. Pressed by his chief adviser Christian of Anhalt, he decided at the end of September to accept. He left Heidelberg on 29 September, entered Prague on 31 October and was crowned in St Vitus Cathedral on 4 November 1619, by Utraquist and Protestant clergy rather than the Catholic archbishop.

His reign was short and troubled. The kingdom's finances were in disorder, neither he nor his queen spoke Czech, and in December 1619 his Calvinist court preacher Abraham Scultetus had images stripped from St Vitus Cathedral, which offended the Utraquist majority. Meanwhile Ferdinand gathered allies: on 21 October 1619 he agreed with Maximilian of Bavaria, leader of the Catholic League, that Maximilian would command against Frederick and receive his electoral title, and the Lutheran Elector of Saxony joined the emperor in return for Lusatia. James I sent no troops, and on 3 July 1620 the Protestant Union declared itself neutral in the Treaty of Ulm, while Spanish troops overran Frederick's own Palatinate on the Rhine.

On 8 November 1620 the imperial and League army destroyed the Bohemian army at the White Mountain outside Prague, and the next day Frederick fled with his family to Breslau, eventually settling at The Hague. Ferdinand declared his lands and titles forfeit in January 1621 (on the 21st according to Wikipedia; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 22 January for the imperial ban), and in 1623 his electoral dignity was given to Maximilian. Mocked from early in his reign as the 'Winter King' for the brevity of his rule, Frederick spent the rest of his life in exile and died at Mainz on 29 November 1632.

Q629302.title: Battle of Lutter
Q629302.place: Lutter am Barenberge, south of Salzgitter, Lower Saxony, Germany
paras: After the Bohemian Revolt was crushed, the Protestant princes of northern Germany feared that Emperor Ferdinand II and the Catholic League would take back the church lands they had secularised. King Christian IV of Denmark was also Duke of Holstein, and so a member of the Lower Saxon Circle of the Empire; in 1625 the Circle chose him to command its forces. He had his own aims too: control of the Elbe and Weser and the secularised bishoprics of Bremen and Verden for his sons, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. With English and Dutch subsidies he took the field against the army of the Catholic League under Count Tilly and a new imperial army raised by Albrecht von Wallenstein.

Christian's plan for 1626 went wrong from the start. His ally Ernst von Mansfeld was beaten by Wallenstein at the Dessau Bridge on the Elbe in April and marched off towards Silesia and Hungary, and Christian of Brunswick's attack failed. In late July the king marched south from Wolfenbüttel to seek battle with Tilly, not knowing, according to Wikipedia, that Wallenstein had sent Tilly more than 4,000 reinforcements. Heavy rain slowed his army while Tilly took the Protestant-held towns of Münden, Northeim and Göttingen. Christian turned back, his rearguard harried by Tilly's cavalry, and on 27 August 1626 he decided to stand and fight at Lutter am Barenberge, behind two small streams, with woods on both flanks.

Wikipedia's account, based on modern military histories, describes the battle as follows. Around midday Tilly's artillery opened fire while his troops seized the bridge in front of the Danish line. When a Danish counter-attack pushed them back, the young commander of Christian's right, Philipp of Hesse-Kassel, took it as the signal for a general advance and charged without orders; the king then committed the rest of his army, but the attack broke down under close-range artillery fire. Both wing commanders, Philipp and Fuchs von Bimbach, were killed. In the late afternoon Tilly attacked across the stream while part of his army came round through the woods into the Danish rear, and the Danish front gave way; cavalry charges covered the escape of the rest, and Christian fled to Wolfenbüttel. The same account puts Danish losses at 3,000 dead or wounded, with another 2,500 who surrendered the next day, against about 700 on Tilly's side, and notes that the 1908 Kriegs-Lexikon of Gaston Bodart gives 7,000 and 2,000. Tilly took all the Danish guns and much of the baggage.

Lutter was a turning point of the Danish phase of the war. Many of Christian's German allies abandoned him, Mansfeld, who had marched on into Hungary, died before the end of 1626, and in 1627 the armies of Tilly and Wallenstein occupied Holstein and the whole of Jutland. Denmark's fleet and an alliance with Sweden kept the war going, but in 1629 Christian made peace at Lübeck, keeping his territory but giving up his involvement in the affairs of the Empire.

Q703097.title: Edict of Restitution
Q703097.place: Vienna (applied across the Holy Roman Empire)
paras: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had let each German ruler decide the religion of his lands, but its 'Ecclesiastical Reservation' forbade the further secularisation of Catholic church lands. Protestant princes read the settlement differently, and in the following decades many bishoprics and religious houses, especially in northern Germany, passed under Protestant control, often through noble families who placed younger sons in them; the emperors were too weak to stop this. By 1628 the Catholic armies of Count Tilly and Albrecht von Wallenstein had beaten the Bohemians, the Palatinate and Denmark, and Catholic claims to lost church property were pouring in to Emperor Ferdinand II. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia he passed them in September 1628 to his Aulic Council, the imperial court, for investigation.

On 6 March 1629 Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution in Vienna. It enforced the emperor's reading of the Ecclesiastical Reservation retroactively. The Catholic Encyclopedia summarises it in three parts: it laid down the meaning of the disputed clauses of the religious peace, ordered that pending lawsuits under the peace be settled summarily according to the edict, and appointed three commissions to find and undo breaches of the peace across the Empire. Its reach is measured differently: Wikipedia says that if fully carried out it would have changed the rulers of the archbishoprics of Bremen and Magdeburg, 12 bishoprics and more than 100 religious houses, while the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says it gave back 150 northern ecclesiastical foundations to the Catholics.

Imperial commissioners began enforcing it at once, backed by Wallenstein's army. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives examples: the Guelph dukes had to surrender most of what they had taken of the diocese of Hildesheim, commissioners took possession of Magdeburg in March 1630, a Catholic bishop installed himself at Verden and Minden, and Württemberg in the south was forced to make restitution. Wikipedia adds that tens of thousands of Protestants fled to Protestant-ruled states.

The edict sharpened the religious side of the war and alienated all the Protestant princes, including the Lutheran electors of Saxony and Brandenburg, who had stood by the emperor during the Bohemian revolt; they stayed away from the Electoral Diet at Regensburg in 1630 in protest. The Catholic princes, for their part, resented Wallenstein, and at Regensburg Ferdinand had to dismiss him in August 1630. Meanwhile Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden had landed in Pomerania. When Ferdinand rejected Saxony's appeal to revoke the edict, the Elector of Saxony took up arms and allied with the Swedes in 1631. The edict was in effect abandoned in the Peace of Prague of 1635, which Wikipedia says set aside its terms.

Q708862.title: Treaty of Lübeck
paras: The Treaty of Lübeck ended the Danish phase of the Thirty Years' War, which King Christian IV of Denmark had entered in 1625 as leader of the Protestant princes of the Lower Saxon Circle. After his defeat by Count Tilly at Lutter in August 1626, the armies of Tilly and of the imperial general Albrecht von Wallenstein overran northern Germany and in 1627 occupied Holstein and the whole Jutland peninsula. Wallenstein, rewarded with the confiscated duchy of Mecklenburg, then turned to the Baltic coast, planning a fleet to challenge Danish sea power.

Denmark's navy kept the Danish islands safe, and in 1628 Christian struck back from the sea, raiding the occupied coasts and destroying Wallenstein's naval works. Christian allied with Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden (on 1 January 1628 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica; Wikipedia puts the alliance in April), and Danish and Swedish help enabled the port of Stralsund to hold out against Wallenstein's siege, which was abandoned in August. Christian's own attempt to land on the southern Baltic shore ended in defeat at Wolgast later that month, and both sides were now ready to talk. Wallenstein feared a joint Danish–Swedish war, and Emperor Ferdinand II's resources were stretched by a new war in northern Italy over the succession to Mantua.

Envoys met at Lübeck in January 1629. According to Wikipedia, an earlier imperial draft had demanded that Christian give up his bishoprics and imperial offices and buy back his occupied provinces, and Christian met Gustavus Adolphus in February 1629 but refused his proposal of a joint invasion under Swedish command. The final terms were settled largely in secret talks with Wallenstein. The treaty was signed on 22 May 1629 by Wallenstein and Christian IV and ratified by Ferdinand on 7 June; the Catholic League was included as a party.

Christian got back all the territory he had lost, including Holstein, Schleswig and Jutland, without paying any war costs; the 1911 Britannica and the Catholic Encyclopedia both note that he lost no land. In return, according to Wikipedia, he gave up his claims to the bishoprics of Lower Saxony (including Bremen and Verden, which he had sought for his sons), ended his alliances with the north German states and promised not to interfere in the affairs of the Empire again. The lenient peace left the north German Protestants unprotected just as Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution in March 1629, and Denmark's place as the leading Protestant power of the north passed to Sweden, whose king landed in Pomerania the following year.

Q7655000.title: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War
Q7655000.place: Northern and southern Germany, from Pomerania to Bavaria
paras: By 1629 Emperor Ferdinand II and the Catholic League seemed to have won the war in Germany: Denmark had made peace at Lübeck, Wallenstein's imperial army held the Baltic coast, and the Edict of Restitution threatened to return a large share of the Protestant-held church lands to Catholic hands. King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden saw the danger both to his fellow Protestants and to Sweden itself. The Catholic Encyclopedia stresses the economic motives: Ferdinand's plans for the Baltic threatened Sweden's copper trade and the customs revenues it drew from its conquests across the sea. Gustavus had been fighting Poland–Lithuania, whose king Sigismund, his Catholic cousin, claimed the Swedish throne with Ferdinand's backing; in September 1629 France helped arrange the Truce of Altmark, which freed him to turn to Germany.

Gustavus landed in Pomerania in the summer of 1630 (in June according to the Catholic Encyclopedia, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia's Thirty Years' War article; in July according to Wikipedia's article on the intervention). He forced the old Duke Bogislav XIV of Pomerania and then, reluctantly, the Elector of Brandenburg into alliance, and in January 1631, short of money, he made the Treaty of Bärwalde with France, pledging to carry on the war against the emperor. At first few German princes joined him, and he could not prevent Tilly from storming and sacking Magdeburg in May 1631. But when Ferdinand refused to revoke the Edict and Tilly invaded Saxony, the Lutheran Elector John George allied with Sweden, and on 17 September 1631 the Swedes and Saxons destroyed Tilly's army at Breitenfeld near Leipzig.

Gustavus then marched not on Vienna but into southern and western Germany, wintering at Mainz among the Catholic bishoprics of the Main and Rhine. In April 1632 he forced the crossing of the Lech against Tilly, who was mortally wounded, and occupied Munich and much of Bavaria, while the Saxons took Prague. Ferdinand recalled Wallenstein, who raised a new army, drove the Saxons from Bohemia and entrenched himself near Nuremberg; Gustavus's assault on his camp at the Alte Veste was repulsed with heavy losses (3 September 1632; the Britannica also gives the Old Style date, 24 August). Wallenstein moved into Saxony, Gustavus followed, and on 16 November 1632 the two armies fought at Lützen near Leipzig. The Swedes held the field, but Gustavus was killed.

Sweden's chancellor Axel Oxenstierna took over the direction of the war, with Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar and Gustav Horn as its generals, and in 1633 formed the League of Heilbronn with the Protestant states of south-western and central Germany. Wallenstein, suspected of treating with the enemy, was murdered at Eger on 25 February 1634. In September 1634 the imperial army under the emperor's son, joined by a Spanish army from Italy under the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand, crushed Horn and Bernhard at Nördlingen; the Britannica says the model army of Gustavus perished there. Saxony made peace with the emperor in the Peace of Prague of 30 May 1635, which most of the German princes accepted and which in effect abandoned the Edict of Restitution. The war did not end: in May 1635 France went openly to war with Spain, and Sweden fought on as France's ally until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which gave it Western Pomerania.

Q698045.title: Sack of Magdeburg
paras: Magdeburg on the Elbe, the seat of a Protestant-ruled archbishopric and one of the largest towns in Germany, had been Lutheran since 1524. The Edict of Restitution of 1629 made its archbishopric one of the chief prizes to be returned to the Catholic Church; Wallenstein had already tried and failed to force a garrison on the city that year. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden's landing in Pomerania in 1630 emboldened the city council. Its deposed Protestant administrator, Christian William of Brandenburg, who had fled to the Swedish king, came back, becoming by the end of the year Sweden's only new German ally, according to Wikipedia, and the Swedish officer Dietrich von Falkenberg arrived to direct its defence (in September 1630 according to the Catholic Encyclopedia, in November according to Wikipedia).

The army of the Catholic League under Count Tilly laid siege to Magdeburg in the spring of 1631, with Gottfried Heinrich zu Pappenheim conducting the siege. Gustavus, unable to march on without the support of Brandenburg and Saxony, could not relieve it. On 20 May 1631 the besiegers stormed the walls after an artillery bombardment, broke in through the defences and killed Falkenberg; that is the date in Wikipedia and the Catholic Encyclopedia, while the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which elsewhere gives this war's dates in two styles ten days apart, has 10 May. The soldiers, long unpaid, plundered the city, and contemporary reports quoted by Wikipedia describe rape, torture and killing. A fire spread through the town and burned almost all of it. Who started it is disputed: Wikipedia says attackers set fire to houses to drive out defenders and that the spread was probably unintended, while the Catholic Encyclopedia says the Swedes were accused of starting it when they saw the city was lost. The cathedral, where about a thousand people had taken refuge, was saved on Tilly's orders, and Tilly ended the looting on 24 May.

The numbers differ by source. Wikipedia counts about 20,000 dead, with only some 5,000 of about 25,000 inhabitants surviving and 1,700 of 1,900 buildings destroyed; the 1911 Britannica says the town had 36,000 inhabitants, the greater part of whom were butchered, and that apart from the cathedral only about 140 houses were left standing. It was the worst massacre of the war, and 'to magdeburgise' became a byword for total destruction.

According to the Britannica the sack paralysed the Protestants, while Catholics rejoiced; Pope Urban VIII and Maximilian of Bavaria sent Tilly letters of congratulation. Gustavus was blamed on all sides for leaving the city to its fate, and the Catholic Encyclopedia judges that the fire cost Tilly the advantage he had won. Within months, the emperor's refusal to drop the Edict and Tilly's invasion of Saxony drove the Elector of Saxony into alliance with Sweden, and in September Tilly was crushed at Breitenfeld. The 1911 Britannica says the city recovered with remarkable speed, while Wikipedia records only 449 inhabitants in a census of 1632 and much of the town still in ruins in 1720.

cp06-12.title: Wallenstein is assassinated
paras: Albrecht von Wallenstein was a Bohemian nobleman, raised a Protestant, who had turned Catholic and made his fortune on the emperor's side in the Bohemian Revolt, acquiring confiscated rebel estates that became his duchy of Friedland. From 1625 he raised and commanded huge armies for Emperor Ferdinand II, paid for by levies on the territories they occupied. His power and his armies' exactions made him many enemies among the German princes, Catholic and Protestant alike, and in 1630 Ferdinand dismissed him. After Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden had beaten Tilly and occupied Munich, the emperor recalled him in 1632 with almost unlimited powers. Wallenstein drove the Saxons out of Bohemia, held off Gustavus at the Alte Veste near Nuremberg and fought the battle of Lützen, where the Swedish king was killed.

In 1633 he did little fighting, apart from a victory over the Swedes at Steinau on the Oder in October, and instead negotiated with Saxony, Brandenburg, Sweden and France. What he intended is unclear. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, followed by Wikipedia, says he wanted to 'force a just peace' on the emperor, including the revocation of the Edict of Restitution; the Catholic Encyclopedia calls the negotiations treason and suggests he was driven largely by a desire for revenge. Spain's envoys pressed the emperor to remove him, and his inactivity alarmed Vienna. On 12 January 1634, at Pilsen, his senior officers signed a declaration of loyalty to him. On 24 January Ferdinand signed a secret patent removing him from command, and on 18 February a patent charging him with high treason was published in Prague. The garrisons of Prague and Pilsen went over to the emperor.

With his command collapsing, Wallenstein left Pilsen on 23 February with a few close followers and, according to the Britannica, about 1,000 men, for Eger (Cheb), hoping to join the Swedes under Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar. At Eger the commandant, Colonel Gordon, and Colonels Butler and Leslie decided to kill him; the Catholic Encyclopedia describes the killers as two Protestant Scottish officers and one Catholic Irish officer of his own army. On the evening of 25 February his chief supporters, Illo, Kinsky, Terzky and Neumann, were received at a banquet by the three colonels and murdered, and soldiers then broke into Wallenstein's lodgings, where, as the Britannica relates, Captain Devereux killed him with a partisan. Most sources date the killing to 25 February 1634; the Catholic Encyclopedia's biography of Wallenstein gives 24 February.

According to the Britannica no direct order for the murder had been given, but it was well understood that his death would be welcome at court, and the killers were richly rewarded. Command of the imperial army passed to the emperor's son Ferdinand, King of Hungary, with Matthias Gallas as its real commander. Without Wallenstein's organisation the emperor came to rely on Spanish help, and in September 1634 the combined imperial and Spanish armies defeated the Swedes at Nördlingen.

Q312212.title: Battle of Nördlingen
paras: After the death of Gustavus Adolphus at Lützen in 1632, Sweden and its German allies of the League of Heilbronn still held much of southern Germany, which cut the Spanish Road, the overland route by which Spain supplied its war against the Dutch. With Wallenstein murdered in February 1634, Emperor Ferdinand II relied more on Spain. His son Ferdinand, King of Hungary, took command of the imperial army, with Matthias Gallas in real command, retook Regensburg and Donauwörth, and laid siege to the Swedish-held town of Nördlingen. On 2 September a Spanish army under the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand, on its way from Italy to the Netherlands, joined him there.

The Swedish commanders, Marshal Gustav Horn and Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar, marched to relieve the town. Horn wanted to wait for reinforcements, but Bernhard pressed for an immediate attack, and they badly underestimated the Spanish force. Wikipedia, drawing on modern studies, puts the Protestant army at about 26,000, including 8,000 poorly trained Württemberg militia, against more than 33,000 Spanish and imperial troops; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls the Catholic army only 'somewhat superior'.

The battle was fought on 5 and 6 September 1634. On the 5th the Protestant army moved onto a line of hills south of the town and fought for them into the night. Early on the 6th Horn's troops repeatedly attacked the Albuch hill, held by veteran Spanish infantry; according to Wikipedia they briefly drove back its defenders, but a Spanish counter-attack restored the line, and assault after assault failed while Gallas and the Spanish commanders kept feeding in fresh troops. When Horn began to pull back, the Spanish and imperial troops advanced, routed Bernhard's cavalry and fell on Horn's men from two sides, and the Swedish army broke up.

Losses are given differently. Wikipedia gives 12,000 to 14,000 Protestant casualties (some sources, it notes, say up to 16,000), including 4,000 prisoners, against 3,500 on the other side; the 1911 Britannica's article on the war gives 17,000 Swedish and allied losses against 2,000, and its article on Nördlingen says Horn was captured with 3,000 men. Bernhard escaped with the survivors to Heilbronn.

Nördlingen ended Swedish power in southern Germany; the Britannica says the model army of Gustavus perished there. The imperial army retook Württemberg, and the Cardinal-Infante went on to the Netherlands. Saxony made peace with the emperor, formalised in the Peace of Prague of May 1635, which most of the German princes accepted. The collapse of Sweden's German alliance brought France openly into the war: in 1635 it made a new alliance with Sweden, paid for an army under Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar, and in May declared war on Spain.

cp18-099.title: Khanate of Kokand founded
paras: In the early 18th century the Uzbek Khanate of Bukhara, ruled by the Ashtarkhanid (Astrakhanid) dynasty, was losing its hold over the valley of the Syr Darya. In the west, Kazakhs held Tashkent and Turkestan; in the east, in the fertile Fergana Valley, power passed to local rulers, among them heads of Khoja (Sufi) families who governed individual towns, while Kyrgyz, Kazakh and Oirat (Dzungar) nomads raided the region.

Wikipedia dates the founding of the Khanate of Kokand to 1709, when Shahrukh Biy, leader of the Ming tribe of Uzbeks, built the fortress of Koktonliq Ata near Kokand and became ruler of the area; he reigned until 1722. The early history is poorly recorded, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes. The 19th-century historian Henry Howorth, relying on traditions preserved by Mahsum Khoja, which he calls unsatisfactory but the only material available, says that Shah Rukh, a man of noble but not royal birth, arrived in Fergana at the beginning of the century, married the daughter of the Khoja ruler of the town of Khurram Serai, settled at Kurkan a few miles west of Kokand, then killed his father-in-law and made himself master of the district.

Shahrukh was succeeded by his eldest son Abd al-Rahim and then by another son, Abd al-Karim. Abd al-Rahim occupied Khujand and Ura-Tyube and, for six months, Samarkand, and Abd al-Karim built the present city of Kokand and made it the capital; Wikipedia dates the new fortress and capital to 1740, while the Britannica says the town was founded by Abd al-Rahim in 1732 under the name of Iski-kurgan. Under Abd al-Karim, Kokand survived invasions by the Dzungars in the 1740s, and his successor Irdana Biy (Erdeni) submitted to the Chinese Qing emperor after the Qing conquest of Dzungaria and East Turkestan in 1758–1759.

Kokand's rulers used the title biy (a form of beg) through the 18th century. In the early 19th century Alim brought the other towns of Fergana under his rule and conquered Tashkent, and under his successors, styled khans, Kokand became a powerful state, which later fought Bukhara and the advancing Russians. Russia annexed the khanate after taking Kokand and Andijan in February 1876, and turned it into the province of Fergana.

Q3178839.title: First voyage of James Cook
Q3178839.place: Pacific Ocean: Tahiti, New Zealand and the east coast of Australia (Botany Bay)
paras: In 1768 the Royal Society asked King George III to fund an expedition to the Pacific to observe the transit of Venus across the Sun, expected on 3 June 1769, which would help astronomers calculate the distance from the Earth to the Sun. The Admiralty combined the scientific mission with a confidential one: to search the South Pacific for the supposed great southern continent, Terra Australis. Command went to James Cook, a former merchant seaman who had made his name as a naval surveyor of the St Lawrence River and Newfoundland and was promoted lieutenant for the voyage. His ship was the Endeavour, a 'North-Country cat' bought by the government, and with him went the astronomer Charles Green and the wealthy naturalist Joseph Banks, who brought the Swedish botanist Daniel Solander and the artists Sydney Parkinson and Alexander Buchan.

The Endeavour left Plymouth in August 1768 (on the 26th according to Wikipedia, the 25th according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica), rounded Cape Horn and reached Tahiti on 13 April 1769. The transit was observed from a small fort at Point Venus on 3 June, but the timings of Cook, Green and Solander differed more than expected and the results proved less exact than hoped. Cook then opened his sealed orders, visited and claimed the neighbouring Society Islands, guided by the Tahitian priest and navigator Tupaia, and sailed south and west. He reached New Zealand in October 1769, the first Europeans there since Abel Tasman in 1642, and spent six months charting both islands and the strait between them, now Cook Strait. Several Māori were killed in the first encounters, which Cook regretted.

Turning west, he sighted the south-east coast of Australia on 19 April 1770 (20 April by today's local calendar) and became the first known European to reach its eastern coast. Near the end of April the ship entered a broad inlet, and Cook's party landed at what is now Botany Bay, on the land of the Gweagal people of the Dharawal. Two Gweagal men tried to drive them off; Cook fired small shot, wounding one, and the men threw spears. The expedition stayed a week, and Banks and Solander's plant collections gave the bay its name. Sailing north along the coast, the Endeavour struck the Great Barrier Reef on 11 June 1770 and was saved only by jettisoning her guns and other weight and patching the hull; repairs took weeks. On 22 August, at Possession Island off Cape York, Cook claimed the whole eastern coast for Great Britain, and by passing through Torres Strait he confirmed that New Guinea was separate from Australia.

Cook had lost no men to scurvy, but at Batavia (Jakarta), where the ship was repaired, malaria and dysentery killed many of the company, among them Tupaia, Green and Parkinson; Wikipedia counts seven dead at Batavia and 23 more on the voyage home. The Endeavour returned by the Cape of Good Hope and anchored in the Downs off Deal on 12 July 1771, according to Wikipedia (the Britannica gives 12 June). The voyage disproved a southern continent north of 40° South, charted New Zealand and eastern Australia with a new accuracy, and led to Cook's second voyage of 1772–1775; Banks later promoted Botany Bay as a place for a British settlement.

cp07-04.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
paras: In the summer of 1789 the deputies of the Estates-General, now the National Constituent Assembly, set out to give France a written constitution. On the night of 4 August they voted to abolish privileges and feudal rights. They decided to begin with a declaration of principles that would stand as the constitution's preamble; the constitutional committee elected on 14 July was told to start by drafting it. The Marquis de Lafayette had prepared a draft in consultation with Thomas Jefferson, then the American envoy in Paris, and the Abbé Sieyès and Mirabeau shaped the final version, which the Assembly debated article by article from a 24-article draft prepared by one of its committees.

The official record printed with the text gives the sessions of 20 to 26 August 1789, and the last article was adopted on 26 August. The preamble declares, 'in the presence and under the auspices of the Supreme Being', that ignorance, neglect or contempt of the rights of man are the sole causes of public misfortune and corrupt government. Its seventeen articles state that men are born and remain free and equal in rights; that the natural rights of man are liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression; that sovereignty resides in the nation; and that law is the expression of the general will, equal for all, with all citizens equally eligible for public office according to their abilities. It forbids arbitrary arrest and retroactive punishment, presumes innocence until guilt is declared, protects opinions, 'even religious ones', as long as they do not disturb public order, and guarantees free speech and printing subject to the law. Taxes must be shared according to means and consented to by the citizens or their representatives; a society without a guarantee of rights or a separation of powers has no constitution; and property is an inviolable and sacred right.

The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the clergy's proposals for articles guaranteeing respect for religion were rejected, leaving only the article on freedom of opinion. On 1 October the Assembly sent its president to present the declaration to Louis XVI for his acceptance; his refusal to promulgate it was one of the grievances behind the march on Versailles that brought the royal family to Paris on 6 October 1789.

The declaration became the preamble of the Constitution of 1791. Its rights were in practice limited: that constitution distinguished 'active' from 'passive' citizens, its rights were given to men only, and it did not abolish slavery in the colonies, though it inspired the slave risings in Saint-Domingue. It had a wide influence on ideas of individual liberty and democracy in Europe and beyond, and it remains part of French constitutional law through the preambles of the constitutions of 1946 and 1958.

Q1192894.title: Flight to Varennes
paras: Since October 1789, when a Paris crowd brought them from Versailles, Louis XVI and his family had lived in the Tuileries Palace in Paris under close watch. The king had accepted much of the Revolution, but the Civil Constitution of the Clergy troubled his conscience, and at Easter 1791 the National Guard stopped him from leaving for Saint-Cloud to spend Easter. Urged on by Marie Antoinette, he resolved to escape to Montmédy near the eastern frontier, where the Marquis de Bouillé commanded troops thought loyal to the crown, and from there to wait for foreign help or a reaction in France. The escape was planned largely by the queen's Swedish friend Count Axel von Fersen and the Baron de Breteuil.

On the night of 20–21 June 1791 the king, the queen, their two children and the king's sister Madame Élisabeth left the Tuileries in disguise: the children's governess, Madame de Tourzel, posed as a Russian baroness and the king as her valet. Louis left behind a declaration complaining of his treatment and disowning the measures he had accepted under constraint. According to Wikipedia, the family refused to split up into light carriages, as Fersen advised, and travelled in a single heavy coach; delays, broken harness and a lack of secrecy put them behind schedule, and the cavalry detachments posted along the road had withdrawn or been neutralised by suspicious crowds. At Sainte-Menehould the postmaster, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, recognised the king, and on 21 June the party was stopped and arrested at Varennes-en-Argonne, about 50 km short of Montmédy. The king's brother, the Count of Provence, who fled the same night by another route, escaped to Brussels.

The family was brought back to Paris on 25 June, met by silent crowds. The Assembly suspended the king from his functions, and the Cordeliers club and others demanded his deposition and trial; a petition at the Champ de Mars on 17 July ended with the National Guard firing on the crowd. The Assembly preferred to keep Louis as a constitutional monarch, and he swore to the new constitution in September 1791 (on the 13th according to the Catholic Encyclopedia and the 1911 Britannica's Louis XVI article, the 14th according to its French Revolution article). But the flight had shown that he did not accept the Revolution, and republicanism grew. When war with Austria went badly, the monarchy fell on 10 August 1792 and was abolished on 21 September; Louis was tried for treason and guillotined in January 1793.

cp07-09.title: French First Republic proclaimed
paras: By the summer of 1792 France's constitutional monarchy was collapsing. Louis XVI's flight to Varennes in June 1791 had destroyed trust in him, and the war against Austria and Prussia begun in April 1792 went badly. In July the Prussian-Austrian commander, the Duke of Brunswick, threatened Paris with destruction if the royal family were harmed. On 10 August 1792 an insurrection stormed the Tuileries Palace, and the Legislative Assembly suspended the king and called elections for a National Convention; the royal family was imprisoned in the Temple. As Prussian troops advanced and took Longwy, prisoners were massacred in Paris in the first days of September; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts the victims at 1,400.

The Convention, elected by almost universal suffrage though with few voters, met in Paris (on 20 September according to the Britannica and Wikipedia's article on the abolition, on 21 September according to the Catholic Encyclopedia), just as the French army under Dumouriez halted the Prussians at Valmy on 20 September. At its session of 21 September, when the deputy Jean-Marie Collot d'Herbois proposed abolishing the monarchy, Abbé Henri Grégoire, the constitutional bishop of Blois, answered a call for debate by asking what need there was of discussion when everyone agreed, and declaring that the history of kings was the martyrology of nations. The abolition of royalty was voted unanimously.

Accounts differ over when the republic itself was proclaimed. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Grégoire proclaimed it at the first session; Wikipedia says it was never formally proclaimed, but that from 22 September the Convention dated its acts from Year I of the Republic and on 25 September declared the Republic 'one and indivisible'; the Britannica's article on the Republican calendar says the republic was proclaimed on 22 September 1792, the day chosen as the start of the new era because it was also that year's autumn equinox.

The new Republic tried and executed Louis XVI in January 1793, fought most of Europe, put down risings such as the one in the Vendée, and passed through the Terror and the Directory. It lasted, in changing forms, until Napoleon was declared Emperor of the French on 18 May 1804.
