Q3062714.title: Execution of Louis XVI
Q3062714.place: Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde), Paris, France
paras: Louis XVI had reigned since 1774. After his failed flight to Varennes in June 1791 he remained king under the new constitution, but the war against Austria declared in 1792 went badly and turned popular anger against him and Queen Marie Antoinette. On 10 August 1792 an insurrection captured the Tuileries Palace and the Legislative Assembly suspended the monarchy; the royal family was imprisoned in the Temple in Paris. On 21 September the newly elected National Convention abolished the monarchy, leaving the question of what to do with the former king.

The Jacobins of the Mountain wanted his death; Robespierre argued that Louis should be condemned without any trial, as a public enemy. The discovery in November of a hidden iron chest of the king's secret papers, which showed that many public men had dealt with the court, turned opinion further against him. The Convention decided on 3 December to try him itself. He was brought before it on 11 December to hear the charges, essentially of plotting against the constitution and the safety of the nation, and his defence was heard on 26 December. In January 1793 no deputy voted that he was not guilty; the Girondins' proposal to put the sentence to the people was defeated by 424 votes to 287 according to Wikipedia (424 to 283 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica), and death was voted by 361 deputies, a majority of one; the Britannica gives 360 against.

Louis was executed on the morning of 21 January 1793. According to Wikipedia's detailed account, he left the Temple in a carriage with his Irish confessor, Henry Essex Edgeworth, through streets lined with tens of thousands of armed men, and reached the Place de la Révolution, the present Place de la Concorde, at about 10:15. At the scaffold he began to declare his innocence to the crowd, but a drum roll drowned his words; the executioner Charles-Henri Sanson worked the guillotine at 10:22, and his head was shown to the crowd, some of whom cheered for the nation and the republic.

The Britannica says the Jacobins wanted the king's death partly to defy Europe and to compromise their more moderate colleagues. The struggle between Jacobins and Girondins went on, and in 1793 the Revolutionary Tribunal began the Reign of Terror. Marie Antoinette was guillotined at the same place on 16 October 1793. Their son, Louis Charles, became 'Louis XVII' to royalists, but the Bourbon monarchy returned only in 1814.

cp18-101.title: Emirate of Bukhara founded
paras: In the 17th and 18th centuries the Uzbek Khanate of Bukhara was ruled by the Janid (Ashtarkhanid) dynasty, the last line descended from Genghis Khan to hold the throne. Real power passed step by step to the ataliqs, chief ministers drawn from the Manghit tribe of Uzbeks. In 1740 the khan Abu'l-Faiz submitted to Nadir Shah of Persia, and after Nadir Shah's death in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had Abu'l-Faiz killed. Wikipedia says the Manghits then ruled through puppet khans; the 19th-century historian Henry Howorth says Muhammad Rahim first set up puppets and then took the throne himself.

According to Howorth, Muhammad Rahim's successor as ataliq, Daniyal Bi, refused the title of khan and put a Janid prince, Abu'l-Ghazi, on the throne, though the khan was a mere figurehead. Daniyal's eldest son Shah Murad, called Beg-i Jan as a boy and later Amir Ma'sum, was devoted to Sufism and religious law. Howorth relates that, offended by the luxury and vice around his father, he had the powerful vizier Devlet Bi put to death and imposed strict religious discipline on the city. Wikipedia dates Daniyal's time as ataliq to 1758–1785; Howorth puts his death, with some doubt, in 1770.

Wikipedia dates the founding of the Emirate to 1785, when Shah Murad took power after his father's death and, in the words of that article, assumed the throne openly after the death of the khan Abu'l-Ghazi, formalising the rule of the Manghit dynasty. Because the Manghits did not descend from Genghis Khan, they based their right to rule on Islam and used the title of emir instead of khan. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica also says the Manghit family seized the throne in 1785, in the person of Mir Ma'sum. Howorth reads the evidence differently: Abu'l-Ghazi remained the nominal khan, coins were struck in his name as late as AH 1200 (1785–86), the Friday prayer was probably still said in his name until he died, and the year of his death is unknown. No coins of Shah Murad are known, and in Howorth's account he called himself only naib (deputy) and never took the title of khan.

Shah Murad, a religious zealot who also proved an able commander, turned against the Shia-ruled oasis of Merv. In 1785 he killed its Qajar governor, Bayram Ali Khan, and Wikipedia says he completed its conquest in 1788; Howorth says he had the weir that watered Merv cut and carried a large part of the population off to Bukhara, 17,000 families by his account. Shah Murad died in December 1799, according to Wikipedia (Howorth gives Rajab 1214, that is 1799, and the 1911 Britannica 1802). His dynasty ruled until 1920: after Russian troops entered Samarkand in May 1868 the emir submitted to Russia, Bukhara became a Russian protectorate in 1873, and in September 1920 the Red Army overthrew the emir and the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic replaced the Emirate.

Q4871927.title: Battle of Nuʻuanu
paras: The Battle of Nuʻuanu, fought on Oʻahu in the spring of 1795, was the decisive battle in the wars of Kamehameha I, ruler of the island of Hawaiʻi, to bring the Hawaiian Islands under one rule. His opponent was Kalanikūpule, son of Kahekili II, who had ruled Oʻahu and Maui. Kahekili died at Waikīkī in 1794 (in July, according to the historian W. D. Alexander), and his realm was divided: Kalanikūpule held Oʻahu, while Kahekili's brother Kaʻeokūlani (Kaeo) ruled Maui and the neighbouring islands.

The two soon fought each other. In November 1794 Kaʻeokūlani set out for Kauaʻi by way of Oʻahu; after a skirmish with Kalanikūpule's warriors and a reconciliation, he learned of a plot among his own men to throw him overboard on the voyage, and turned instead to march overland against his nephew. Kalanikūpule was helped by the British trader Captain William Brown, whose ships Jackal and Prince Lee Boo lay in Honolulu harbour, and by some of his seamen, and in December 1794 Kaʻeokūlani was defeated and killed. Soon afterwards Kalanikūpule's men seized Brown's two ships and killed Brown (on 1 January 1795, according to Alexander), and Kalanikūpule set out to attack Kamehameha with the ships. The crews, however, rose at night while the ships lay off Waikīkī, put the king ashore, and sailed to Hawaiʻi, where they told Kamehameha what had happened.

Kamehameha now gathered the largest army the islands had seen. The figures differ: Wikipedia's article on the battle gives about 12,000 men and 1,200 war canoes, its article on Kamehameha 10,000 soldiers and 960 canoes, and Alexander mentions a tradition of 16,000 men. Foreigners in his service, among them John Young, handled his cannon. In February 1795 he took Maui and then Molokaʻi. On the way to Oʻahu one of his leading chiefs, Kaʻiana, who believed that his rivals at Kamehameha's court were plotting against him, deserted with his followers and joined Kalanikūpule.

Kamehameha landed near Waiʻalae and Waikīkī and advanced up the Nuʻuanu Valley, where Kalanikūpule had prepared his positions. At Laʻimi the Oʻahu army resisted until Kaʻiana was killed (by a cannon-ball, according to Alexander) and then gave way. Pursued up the valley, many of the defenders were driven over the Nuʻuanu Pali, the cliff at its head; Wikipedia puts the number who fell or jumped at over 700. Wikipedia dates the battle to May 1795; Alexander's narrative places it about the end of April.

Kalanikūpule escaped, but after months in the mountains he was captured and sacrificed to Kamehameha's war god. Kamehameha divided the lands of Oʻahu among his followers and was now master of all the islands except Kauaʻi and Niʻihau. A first attempt to invade Kauaʻi failed in 1796, when he lost many canoes to strong winds and rough seas in the channel, and in 1810 Kaumualiʻi, king of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, submitted to him, completing the unification of the islands under Kamehameha's rule.

Q219817.title: The French Directory takes power
paras: After the fall of Robespierre in July 1794 the National Convention, now led by moderate republicans, set out to give France a stable government that would prevent both a return of the Terror and the restoration of the monarchy. The result was the Constitution of the Year III, largely the work of Pierre Daunou and Boissy d'Anglas. It created a legislature of two houses: a Council of Five Hundred, which proposed laws, and a Council of Ancients of 250 members aged at least forty, which approved or rejected them. Executive power went to a Directory of five men, chosen by the Ancients from a list drawn up by the Five Hundred, with one director retiring each year. The directors had no voice in legislation, and deputies were chosen by indirect election, with a property qualification for electors in place of universal suffrage. Boissy d'Anglas argued that five members were strong enough to act firmly but too divided for any one of them to become a tyrant.

Unpopular, and fearing for their own safety and their work if the voters turned them out, the members of the Convention decreed that two-thirds of the first legislature must come from their own ranks. The constitution was put to the voters, with few taking part: Wikipedia gives 1,057,390 votes in favour and 49,978 against, out of about five million eligible, while the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 1,050,000 for and only 5,000 against. It was proclaimed in force on 23 September 1795. The two-thirds rule angered royalists and other opponents in Paris, who rose in arms; on 13 Vendémiaire (5 October 1795) troops commanded for the government by the young General Napoleon Bonaparte, under Paul Barras, crushed the insurrection.

The elections for the new councils followed in October. The Convention held its last session at the end of the month (Wikipedia dates it to 25 October, the Britannica to the 26th), and Wikipedia dates the Directory's government from 26 October. To protect the Revolution, the deputies required that all five directors be former members of the Convention who had voted for the execution of Louis XVI. On 31 October the Ancients chose the directors from the Five Hundred's list; the Abbé Sieyès refused the post, and Lazare Carnot was elected in his place. The first Directory thus consisted of Barras, Jean-François Rewbell, Louis-Marie de La Révellière-Lépeaux, Étienne-François Le Tourneur and Carnot. According to Wikipedia they moved into the Luxembourg Palace, where nothing had been prepared for them, and divided the work: Rewbell took foreign affairs, Carnot and Le Tourneur military matters, La Révellière religion and education, and Barras internal affairs.

The new government began with an empty treasury and worthless paper money, and from the start it was split: the Britannica describes Rewbell, Barras and La Révellière as sharing the Jacobin spirit, while Carnot and Le Tourneur favoured more moderate policies. The Directory fought on against the European coalitions, and its general Bonaparte conquered much of Italy. After four years of war, financial crisis and political coups, Bonaparte, back from Egypt, overthrew it in the coup of 18 Brumaire (9 November 1799) and replaced it with the Consulate.

Q974166.title: Battle of Montenotte
paras: In the spring of 1796 the French Directory gave General Napoleon Bonaparte his first army command, the Army of Italy, stationed on the Ligurian coast of the Mediterranean. His troops were hungry, unpaid and poorly equipped. Facing them in the Apennine mountains were two allied armies: an Austrian army under Johann Peter Beaulieu, and the army of the Kingdom of Sardinia (Piedmont) under Michelangelo Alessandro Colli, an Austrian general on loan to Sardinia. The two allies distrusted each other and did not agree on a joint plan. Bonaparte intended to drive a wedge between them and defeat each in turn.

Beaulieu moved first. Believing that the main French force was near Genoa, he attacked an isolated French brigade under Jean-Baptiste Cervoni at Voltri on 10 April; it escaped along the coast to Savona. Meanwhile the Austrian right wing under Eugène-Guillaume Argenteau advanced against the French outposts in the hills above Savona. On 11 April, a day later than planned, it attacked the redoubt on Monte Negino (also called Monte Legino), held by a few French battalions under Colonel Antoine-Guillaume Rampon, who made his men vow to win or die there; the Austrian attacks failed.

Bonaparte at once concentrated superior numbers against Argenteau. Marching through the night and in rain and mist, Amédée Laharpe's division joined Rampon on the mountain, while André Masséna swung round the weak Austrian right towards Montenotte, and Pierre Augereau's division moved towards the Austrians' line of retreat. On 12 April Masséna's attack broke the Austrian right, and Argenteau ordered a retreat towards Dego; his units were badly cut up and scattered, and the next morning he reported only 700 men with the colours. Losses are disputed: according to Wikipedia the Austrians admitted 696 killed, wounded and missing, while several modern historians give about 2,500. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the French at first believed they had beaten Beaulieu's main army, when in fact only part of Argenteau's force had been defeated.

Montenotte was the opening victory of Bonaparte's Italian campaign. It opened a gap between the Austrian and Sardinian armies, and in the following days he fought at Millesimo and Dego and pushed the Sardinians back to Mondovì. Sardinia then signed the Armistice of Cherasco (on 28 April according to Wikipedia, the 27th according to the Britannica), leaving Bonaparte free to turn on the Austrians, whom he drove out of Lombardy. The campaign in Italy ended the War of the First Coalition the following year.

Q17502440.title: Haitian Declaration of Independence
paras: The French colony of Saint-Domingue, on the western part of the island of Hispaniola, was worked by enslaved Africans. In August 1791 the slaves rose in revolt, and in 1793 French commissioners proclaimed the abolition of slavery. By 1801 the former slave Toussaint Louverture controlled the colony and issued a constitution that made him governor for life. Napoleon Bonaparte, then First Consul of France, sent an expedition under his brother-in-law General Charles Leclerc in 1802 to restore French rule; Wikipedia and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica say the aim included restoring slavery. Toussaint laid down his arms on French guarantees, was seized and sent to France, and died in prison there in 1803.

The struggle was renewed under Jean-Jacques Dessalines, one of Toussaint's generals and himself a former slave. His Indigenous Army defeated the French under Rochambeau at Vertières, near Cap-Français, on 18 November 1803, and the French evacuated the colony that month.

On 1 January 1804, at Gonaïves, Dessalines and his generals proclaimed independence and gave the country the name Hayti, after the island's indigenous Taíno name. The printed act, drafted by Dessalines's secretary Louis Boisrond-Tonnerre, has three parts. In the first, the assembled generals swore to renounce France forever and to die rather than live under its rule. The second, Dessalines's proclamation to the people, declares that it is not enough to have expelled the 'barbarians' who had bloodied the land for two centuries, and that the people must 'live independent or die'. It recalls French cruelties and calls for vengeance on the French, but also asks Haitians to leave the neighbouring islands in peace and not to act as revolutionary firebrands there. In the third, seventeen generals proclaimed Dessalines governor-general for life, swore to obey his laws blindly, and gave him the right to make peace and war and to name his successor.

Haiti thus became the first independent state of Latin America and the Caribbean, and the second in the Americas after the United States, born from a successful slave revolt. Between February and April 1804 Dessalines had the remaining white French population massacred; Wikipedia puts the dead at between 3,000 and 5,000. In September 1804 he was proclaimed emperor, and he was crowned in October; he was assassinated in 1806. France did not recognise Haiti's independence until 1825, and the United States not until 1862.

cp07-20.title: Coronation of Napoleon
paras: On 18 May 1804 the French Senate vested the government of the Republic in an emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte, until then First Consul, and a popular vote approved the new Empire by a large majority. Napoleon wanted a coronation that would give his new dynasty legitimacy and prestige, above all among royalists and Catholics; the historian J. Holland Rose argues that receiving the holy oil and the pope's blessing was his best hope of drawing royalists away from the exiled Bourbon king. He therefore insisted that Pope Pius VII come to Paris. According to Rose, the pope was troubled at crowning the man responsible for the execution of the Duc d'Enghien, but was persuaded that religion would gain from his presence.

Napoleon met the pope on the road between Fontainebleau and Nemours, staged as a chance encounter during a hunt, so as to avoid awkward questions of ceremony. Napoleon and Josephine had been married only in a civil ceremony; on the pope's insistence, Cardinal Fesch, Napoleon's uncle, married them privately in a religious rite shortly before the coronation (on the evening before, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica; two days before, according to Rose).

The coronation took place in the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris on 2 December 1804. Instead of the old rite of the French kings at Reims, Napoleon had a new ceremony arranged that combined the Roman liturgy with French royal elements. The pope anointed both the Emperor and Josephine and blessed the regalia, including a new crown made to look medieval and called the Crown of Charlemagne, since the old royal crown had been destroyed in the Revolution. When the moment of crowning came, Napoleon waved the pope aside and placed the crown on his own head.

The ceremony was meant to proclaim a new imperial monarchy: its symbols, such as the golden bees on the coronation mantles, looked back past the Bourbons to the early Frankish kings, and Rose sees in it Napoleon's ambition to appear as the successor of Charlemagne. Wikipedia describes it as a deliberate piece of modern propaganda. In May 1805 Napoleon was crowned again, this time with the Iron Crown of Lombardy as King of Italy, in Milan Cathedral.

Q19902208.title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
paras: The Holy Roman Empire traced its origin to the crowning of Charlemagne by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800, and for a thousand years its emperors claimed to be the first rulers of Christendom. By the 18th century it had no standing army or treasury of its own, and its elected emperors could not exercise effective central control over the German princes. The wars with revolutionary and Napoleonic France proved fatal to it. When Napoleon made himself Emperor of the French in 1804, Francis II answered by taking the additional title of Emperor of Austria for his hereditary lands. After Austria's defeat at Austerlitz in December 1805 and the Peace of Pressburg, the Empire existed little more than in name.

In July 1806 Bavaria, Baden, Württemberg and a number of smaller German princes, under pressure from Napoleon, formed the Confederation of the Rhine, an alliance under his protection outside the Empire (Wikipedia dates its founding treaty to 12 July; the historian J. Holland Rose says the Act was signed in Paris on 17 July). On 22 July, according to Wikipedia, Napoleon demanded that Francis abdicate by 10 August. On 1 August a French envoy informed the Imperial Diet at Regensburg (Ratisbon) that Napoleon no longer recognised the existence of the Empire.

Francis had already decided in June to abdicate when it best suited Austria. His government concluded that the abdication must be combined with the dissolution of the whole Empire: otherwise, Wikipedia explains, the imperial vicars Saxony and Bavaria, both aligned with Napoleon, would govern during the vacancy, and Napoleon might take the imperial title himself, leaving Francis as his vassal. On the morning of 6 August 1806 the imperial herald read Francis's proclamation from the balcony of the Church of the Nine Choirs of Angels in Vienna. Francis laid down the imperial crown and released the electors, princes and estates of the Empire from all their duties and obligations to it. The proclamation did not mention the French ultimatum; it said that the way the German states interpreted the Peace of Pressburg had made it impossible for him to carry out his duties as emperor.

Earlier emperors had abdicated, but this abdication also ended the Empire itself, so that no successor could be elected. In Vienna the news was received with dismay, and lawyers of the time held that, while the emperor could lawfully resign, he had no right to dissolve the Empire. Francis went on ruling his hereditary lands as Emperor Francis I of Austria, while Napoleon, as protector of the Confederation of the Rhine, dominated much of central and southern Germany. After Napoleon's fall the Congress of Vienna did not restore the Empire, but replaced it in 1815 with a looser German Confederation led by Austria.

Q2670007.title: Portuguese court moves to Brazil
paras: By his Berlin Decree of November 1806 Napoleon ordered all continental states to close their ports to British ships. Portugal, Britain's old ally, was ruled by the Prince Regent John (the future King John VI) on behalf of his mentally ill mother, Queen Maria I, and refused to comply. France and Spain then agreed to partition Portugal, by a secret treaty signed at Fontainebleau on 27 October 1807 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and General Junot marched across Spain with a French army (30,000 men, by the Britannica's figure) and Spanish auxiliaries, moving so fast that no effective resistance could be organised.

Rather than be deposed, John decided to move the court to Brazil, Portugal's largest colony. He appointed a council of regency to govern Portugal in his absence. On 27 November the royal family, the court and senior officials boarded the ships (Wikipedia's article gives their number as nearly 10,000 in one place and 15,000 in another), and on 29 November the fleet sailed from the Tagus, escorted by a British squadron under Sir Sidney Smith. Junot entered Lisbon at the end of November.

The court reached Salvador in January 1808, where John opened Brazil's ports to the trade of friendly nations, ending Portugal's monopoly of the colony's commerce, and then settled at Rio de Janeiro, which became the capital of the Portuguese monarchy. The court founded schools, a printing press, a botanical garden and the Bank of Brazil. In 1815 John raised Brazil to a kingdom equal in rank to Portugal, in a United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves (by a decree of 16 December 1815 according to Wikipedia; the Britannica dates it to 16 January 1815), and on Queen Maria's death in 1816 he became king of the united realm.

In Portugal, meanwhile, discontent grew at the king's absence and at British influence, and after the liberal revolution that began at Oporto in 1820, John was obliged to return. He left his son Pedro to govern Brazil and sailed in April 1821, landing in Portugal in July. When the Portuguese Cortes tried to restore Brazil's former colonial status, Pedro sided with the Brazilians and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor of Brazil.

Q1145411.title: Grito de Dolores
paras: When Napoleon overthrew the Spanish Bourbons in 1808 and made his brother Joseph king of Spain, the colony of New Spain (Mexico) refused to accept the French ruler. Its American-born (criollo) leaders sought self-government in the name of the deposed Ferdinand VII, but the European-born Spaniards, fearing the loss of their privileges, overthrew the viceroy in a coup. Creole conspiracies followed, among them one at Querétaro, organised by the corregidor (magistrate) Miguel Domínguez and his wife Josefa Ortiz de Domínguez and joined by militia officers such as Ignacio Allende, Juan Aldama and Mariano Abasolo. Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, the parish priest of the small town of Dolores in Guanajuato, known for promoting new crafts and industries among his parishioners, became part of it.

In September 1810 the plot was discovered and Domínguez was arrested, but Hidalgo was warned in time and the conspirators decided to rise at once. On the night of 15–16 September Hidalgo sent armed men, among them Allende and Abasolo, to free the prisoners in the Dolores jail, rang the church bell, and early on 16 September called on the crowd gathered before his church to rise against the Spanish authorities. His exact words are not known; according to one participant, Juan Aldama, the cry was 'Long live America! Long live religion, and death to bad government!'

Hidalgo and Allende left Dolores with about 800 men, according to Wikipedia, and a great mass of followers, mostly poor and many of them Indians, soon gathered round them. At the shrine of Atotonilco Hidalgo took an image of the Virgin of Guadalupe as his banner. The insurgents took San Miguel, Celaya and Guanajuato, where they stormed the fortified granary of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas and killed many of those who had taken refuge there, and advanced towards Mexico City, but Hidalgo turned back.

Defeated at Aculco in November 1810 and decisively at the Bridge of Calderón near Guadalajara on 17 January 1811 by the royalist general Félix Calleja, Hidalgo fled north, was captured, tried at Chihuahua, stripped of his priesthood and shot (on 30 July 1811 according to Wikipedia; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 31 July or 1 August). The war was continued by José María Morelos and others, and Mexico won its independence in 1821. The 16th of September became Mexico's Independence Day, and every year on its eve the president repeats the cry from the balcony of the National Palace in Mexico City, ringing the bell Hidalgo used in 1810.

Q5915169.title: Independence of Paraguay
paras: Paraguay was a province of the Spanish Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, governed from Buenos Aires. After the May Revolution of 1810 in Buenos Aires, the new junta there claimed authority over the whole viceroyalty and sent an envoy to Asunción, but the Spanish governor, Bernardo de Velasco, called an assembly of local notables, which declared continued loyalty to King Ferdinand VII and rejected the junta's authority. Buenos Aires then sent an army under General Manuel Belgrano to bring Paraguay into line, but in early 1811 Paraguayan militia, led largely by local criollo officers, defeated it at Paraguarí and Tacuarí, while Velasco himself fled from the battlefield.

The victories strengthened the confidence of the Paraguayan-born officers, led by Fulgencio Yegros and Pedro Juan Caballero, and when Velasco began negotiating with the Portuguese in Brazil, Paraguay's old enemies, for military protection, they decided to act. On the evening of 14 May 1811 officers led by Caballero seized the barracks in Asunción and demanded that Velasco share power. When more troops arrived and trained cannon on the government house, Velasco gave in early on 15 May, a day now celebrated as Paraguay's Independence Day. A junta of three was formed: Velasco, the lawyer José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia and the Spanish-born captain Juan Valeriano de Zeballos.

Velasco, suspected of continuing to conspire with the Portuguese, was put under house arrest in June, and a first national congress replaced the junta with a five-man governing junta under Yegros. Francia, who according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica served as secretary to the junta, had an influence far greater than his office. Paraguay refused to submit to Buenos Aires, proposing instead a confederation of independent states. A second congress in October 1813 proclaimed the Republic of Paraguay and entrusted power to two consuls, Yegros and Francia; a third, in October 1814, made Francia sole dictator, at first for three years and later for life.

Under Francia, who ruled until his death in 1840, Paraguay was kept almost entirely isolated from the outside world and avoided war with its neighbours. A formal act of independence was declared only on 25 November 1842, and recognition came slowly: Brazil recognised Paraguay in 1844, but Argentina did so in practice only in 1856.

Q3382350.title: Venezuelan Declaration of Independence
paras: In 1808 Napoleon forced the Spanish kings Charles IV and Ferdinand VII to abdicate at Bayonne and made his brother Joseph king of Spain. In the Spanish colonies the question arose of who now held authority. In Caracas, on 19 April 1810, an open meeting of the town council deposed the Spanish captain general, Vicente Emparán, and set up a Supreme Junta that governed in the name of Ferdinand VII. Most Venezuelan provinces followed, but Maracaibo, Coro and Guayana stayed loyal to the Spanish authorities, and fighting broke out between the two sides.

The junta called a congress of the provinces, which met from March 1811. The returned exile Francisco de Miranda, elected a deputy, and a group of radicals organised in a club modelled on the Jacobins pressed for a complete break with Spain. On 5 July 1811 the congress voted for independence, 40 votes to 4 according to Wikipedia. The declaration, written mainly by Juan Germán Roscio and Cristóbal Mendoza, was issued in the name of seven provinces: Caracas, Cumaná, Barinas, Margarita, Barcelona, Mérida and Trujillo, which formed an American Confederation of Venezuela. It argued that America had recovered its right to govern itself through the abdications at Bayonne, that it was absurd for a vast and populous continent to depend on a small corner of Europe, and that the Spanish governments had treated Venezuela as rebels despite its loyalty. It declared the united provinces free, sovereign and independent states, released from all submission to the Spanish Crown, with full power to choose their own form of government, make war and peace, and conclude alliances and treaties. Miranda was among the signatories.

Venezuela was thus the first Spanish American colony to declare independence. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the proclamation to 14 July 1811; the signed act itself is dated 5 July, which Venezuela celebrates as its Independence Day. A federal constitution followed in December 1811, but the new republic was weak: it was short of money, its paper currency lost value, and it failed to win over the poorer classes. In 1812 a Spanish naval officer, Domingo de Monteverde, raised a royalist army from Coro, and a severe earthquake on 26 March 1812, which struck mainly republican areas, was taken by many as a divine judgement. Miranda, made commander with dictatorial powers, capitulated to Monteverde on 25 July 1812, ending the First Republic. The war for independence went on under Simón Bolívar until the battle of Carabobo in 1821, and, according to the Britannica, Spain recognised Venezuela's independence only in 1845.

Q3248484.title: Argentine Declaration of Independence
paras: The May Revolution of 1810 in Buenos Aires had removed the Spanish viceroy of the Río de la Plata and put a governing junta in his place, but for six years the provinces did not formally break with Spain. By 1815 their position was dangerous: Ferdinand VII, restored to the Spanish throne in 1814, was determined to recover the colonies, royalist armies from Peru had defeated the patriots in Upper Peru (now Bolivia) and threatened the north, and the provinces were divided among themselves. After a revolt in April 1815 removed the Supreme Director Carlos María de Alvear, a general congress was summoned.

The congress opened in March 1816 at San Miguel de Tucumán, in the north-west, with 33 deputies (Wikipedia gives 24 March as the opening date, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 25 March). The provinces of José Gervasio Artigas's Federal League, among them the Banda Oriental (now Uruguay), Santa Fe and Entre Ríos, were not represented, and Paraguay had already gone its own way, while several provinces of Upper Peru did send deputies. The congress named Juan Martín de Pueyrredón Supreme Director, and on 9 July 1816, under the presidency of Francisco Narciso de Laprida, deputy for San Juan, it declared the independence of the United Provinces of South America.

According to Wikipedia, the declaration rested on the argument used by other Spanish American declarations, such as Venezuela's: that when Ferdinand VII was deposed by Napoleon in 1808, sovereignty had returned to the peoples of Spanish America, dissolving their union with Spain. The name United Provinces of South America was chosen in the hope of drawing in other independence movements that were not represented. The declaration was also translated into Quechua and Aymara.

Independence did not end the provinces' divisions. The congress moved to Buenos Aires in 1817 and drew up a centralist constitution in 1819, but it was rejected, and the congress was dissolved in 1820 after the Federal League provinces defeated the national army at Cepeda, beginning years of conflict between centralists (Unitarians) and federalists. The war against Spain continued: San Martín's army, crossing from the Argentine provinces, won the battles of Chacabuco in 1817 and Maipú in 1818 in Chile. Spain recognised Argentine independence only much later: in 1857 according to Wikipedia, in 1842 according to the Britannica.

Q1425658.title: Battle of Chacabuco
paras: Chile's first bid for self-government, begun in 1810, ended in 1814 when a royalist army sent by the viceroy of Peru crushed the patriots at Rancagua, and many of them, including Bernardo O'Higgins, fled across the Andes to Mendoza in Argentina. There the Argentine general José de San Martín, governor of the province of Cuyo, was preparing a larger plan: to defeat Spanish power at its centre in Lima by first freeing Chile and then attacking Peru by sea. With O'Higgins he spent about two years raising and training the Army of the Andes from Argentines and Chilean exiles, while the people of Mendoza made gunpowder, ammunition and even cannon for it.

In January 1817 the army set out across the Andes in two main columns, through the Los Patos and Uspallata passes, crossing passes 13,000 feet high according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Wikipedia's article on the crossing and the Britannica both put the fighting force at about 4,000 men (the Britannica: some 3,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry). San Martín's feints misled the royalist governor, Casimiro Marcó del Pont, about where the blow would fall, so the crossing was not opposed, though many men and more than half the horses were lost on the way.

To delay the patriots, a royalist force of about 1,500 men under Brigadier Rafael Maroto took position at Chacabuco, a valley north of Santiago. San Martín attacked on 12 February 1817, dividing his army in two: one division under O'Higgins was to strike from the front while Miguel Estanislao Soler's division came round the royalist flank and rear. O'Higgins attacked before Soler was in place and was hard pressed, but when Soler arrived and took a royalist artillery position, the royalists were surrounded around the Chacabuco ranch and destroyed. Wikipedia gives royalist losses as 500 killed and 600 captured, against 12 patriots killed in battle and 120 who later died of wounds; Maroto escaped.

The patriots entered Santiago, and when San Martín declined the leadership, O'Higgins was made Supreme Director of Chile. The royalists still held the south, and a new army under Mariano Osorio defeated San Martín at Cancha Rayada, but his victory at Maipú in April 1818 secured Chilean independence and opened the way for his expedition to Peru.

Q1073849.title: Battle of Maipú
paras: After the patriot victory at Chacabuco in February 1817, José de San Martín's Army of the Andes held Santiago, and Bernardo O'Higgins governed Chile as Supreme Director; according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, he formally proclaimed Chile's independence in February 1818. The viceroy of Peru made one more attempt to recover the country, sending an army under General Mariano Osorio, the victor of Rancagua in 1814. Osorio surprised San Martín's army at Cancha Rayada and defeated it, but the patriots regrouped within days, collected weapons in Santiago and trained new recruits at the Ochagavía camp south of the city.

The two armies met on the plain of Maipú, just south of Santiago, with about 5,000 men each according to Wikipedia. Osorio's royalists were drawn up on a ridge near the Lo Espejo farm. The battle began with an artillery duel around 11:30 in the morning, after which San Martín sent the divisions of Las Heras and Alvarado forward against the royalist wings, while patriot cavalry drove off the royalist horse. When the royalist centre under Ordóñez pushed the patriot line back, San Martín sent in his reserve, which broke two royalist battalions. Osorio left the field; Ordóñez made a last stand in the buildings of Lo Espejo, which were shelled by the patriot artillery until he surrendered.

Wikipedia gives royalist losses as about 1,500 killed and 2,289 captured, and patriot losses as 800 killed and 1,000 wounded. The battle is dated 5 April 1818 by Wikipedia (and by Chile's yearly commemoration) and 3 April 1818 in the Britannica's article on Chile. O'Higgins arrived with militia, who rounded up scattered royalist soldiers, and his embrace with San Martín, the 'Abrazo de Maipú', is commemorated in both Chile and Argentina.

Maipú ended major Spanish operations in Chile and secured its independence. It left San Martín free to organise, with O'Higgins and the Argentine government, a fleet and army for the invasion of Peru, which, the Britannica says, set out in August 1820.
